summary.title: SPEC CPU 2026 Run and Reporting Rules
summary.one_liner: You learn the official rules for building, running, and reporting SPEC CPU 2026 benchmark results, including base versus peak, benchmark specials, power measurement, and estimates.
keywords: how are spec cpu results reported
takeaways: Base metrics use one common set of strict optimization flags across all benchmarks, while peak metrics allow per-benchmark tuning.
A 'benchmark special' is a performance method narrowly tuned to a SPEC benchmark; rule 1.4.2 gives objective tests (A and B) and subjective indicators (C and D) to identify one.
Results must be reproducible with obtainable components and fully disclosed; SPEC CPU publishes no independent audit but encourages peer review.
Energy metrics cannot be estimated and are not allowed for cloud bare-metal systems, while performance metrics may be estimated if clearly labeled.
Changes from CPU 2017 include SPECspeed 2026 threading flags (OpenMP, C++ threads, Fortran do concurrent), a Compiler Category field, and an 18.0°C minimum ambient temperature for power measurement.
summary.summary: This page is the official run and reporting rules document for SPEC CPU 2026, the benchmark suite of 52 benchmarks in four suites (SPECspeed and SPECrate, Integer and Floating Point). It opens with a philosophy section defining what a published result is: a performance observation, a declaration of reproducible performance, and a claim about mature methods. The rest of the document covers build rules (section 2), run rules including threading and run-time dynamic optimization (section 3), disclosure and metrics (section 4), and the rules for estimates and non-compliant results (section 5). It also lists changes from SPEC CPU 2017.
